Recent reports suggest that inter-state conflict will break out due to a decline in global fish stocks, while others suggest that ‘the world is already at war over fish’. That commentary draws on the notion of resource wars, which suggests that states often enter into conflict for control of resources, such as oil, gas or precious minerals. The commentators suggest that since fish stocks are declining, it is only a matter of time before the supply of fish also becomes an increasingly valuable resource worth going to war over.

While the International Food Policy Research Institute maintains that ‘food insecurity can be both a cause and consequence of conflict’, the debate about food insecurity causing conflict continues unabated. Other research suggests that food insecurity, on its own, does not automatically lead to a heightened risk of conflict. Other factors, such as the strength of political institutions, also play a decisive role in whether conflict occurs. A review of the linkages between food security and conflict, concludes that it is difficult to isolate the particular factors that contribute to the outbreak of conflict. It suggests that ‘more and better data on and from conflict zones is required for understanding and monitoring the full diversity, nature and interrelations of food security and violent conflict’.

China is often cited as the most likely belligerent in any so-called “fish war”. Some strategic analysts argue that China sees wild fish as ‘a strategic commodity to be protected and defended, if necessary, by force’; they point to the militarisation of the East and South China seas as evidence. An increased Chinese military presence in those regions is not likely to be solely due to the presence of fish, however, and securing strategic maritime trade routes is likely to be an equal, if not greater, motivating factor. Chinese fishing vessels have been found as far afield as Argentina, Ecuador and South Africa. Each of those countries has raised concerns with Beijing about its fishing fleet encroaching on their exclusive economic zones (EEZ). Since 2014, Indonesia has destroyed several Chinese fishing vessels, among hundreds of others, mainly from South-East Asian countries. Food security is not the primary motive for these actions however, as sovereignty and the potential economic loss from increased competition for fish in EEZs, play a larger role in any such “conflict”. In the Indonesian case, the destruction of foreign fishing vessels is designed more to deter illegal fishing that deprives the state of revenue and to boost popular support for the fisheries minister, than to ensure food security.

As declining global fish stocks drive fishing vessels into the exclusive economic zones of other states, the risk of misunderstandings increases. States that feel that their sovereignty is being challenged could retaliate with force, potentially escalating disputes between fishing vessels into armed conflict.
